translations.text: Truly, every man needs to look after his soul's journey himself, and to think how grave it will be when death comes and sunders the kinship of those who were together before, body and soul!
It will be long afterwards that the spirit receives from God himself either punishment or glory, just as that earthen vessel earlier earned for it in the world.

The spirit must come, crying out in its sorrows, always after seven nights, to find the body that it had long worn before, for three hundred years, unless the eternal Lord, almighty God, brings about the end of the world before then.

Then, full of care, it calls in a cold voice; the spirit speaks grimly to the dust: "Listen, you dry and dreary thing, why did you torment me? You filth of the earth, wholly withering away, image of clay!
You gave little thought to what would become of your soul's journey afterwards, once it had been led out of the body!
Very often it seemed to me that it would be thirty thousand years until your death-day. Listen, I waited for our parting in hardship. Now the end is not too good!
You were proud with feasting and sated with wine, and you swaggered in your glory, while I thirsted for God's body, the spirit's drink.
If you had then considered here in life, while I had to dwell in you in the world, that you were strongly driven by the flesh and by sinful lusts, and yet were established through me,
and that I was a spirit in you sent from God, you would never have prepared such hard torments of hell for me through the lust of your needs.
Yet now you must suffer the shame of my disgraces on the great day, when the Only-begotten gathers all mankind together.

Now you are no dearer to anyone living, to any person as a companion, neither to mother nor father nor any kinsman, than the black raven is, since I alone journeyed out of you by the hand of the very one by whom I had earlier been sent in.

[?] and opens the way to the carrion-feast for others, and eats through the eyes from above into the head as a feast for worms, when the accursed body that he long before clothed with garments has grown cold.
